title: The Eminence in Shadow: Exploiting Feature Boundary Ambiguity for Robust Backdoor Attacks

problem.claim: Deep neural networks remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, while existing attacks typically rely on heuristic brute-force methods.

gap.claim: Insufficient rigorous theoretical analysis limits understanding of backdoor mechanisms and constrains attack predictability and adaptability.

contributions.claim: The paper analyzes how sparse decision boundaries enable disproportionate model manipulation and derives a closed-form ambiguous boundary region.
The paper proposes Eminence, an explainable and robust black-box backdoor framework using a universal, visually subtle trigger to exploit vulnerable decision boundaries.
The paper uses influence-function analysis to quantify parameter shifts caused by margin samples and relate them to low poison rates with minimal clean-accuracy impact.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that Eminence achieves robust misclassification with poison rates of at most 0.01%, compared with at least 1% for typical state-of-the-art methods.
The authors report comprehensive experiments supporting their theoretical discussion and an exponential relationship between margin poisoning and adversarial boundary manipulation.
The authors report at least a 90% attack success rate, negligible clean-accuracy loss, and high transferability across models, datasets, and scenarios.

narrative_sequence.summary: DNNs are important but vulnerable to backdoor attacks that commonly use heuristic brute-force methods.
Limited theoretical analysis hinders understanding, predictability, and adaptability of backdoor attacks.
The authors analyze sparse decision boundaries, derive an ambiguous boundary region, and quantify parameter shifts from margin samples.
The authors propose Eminence, an explainable black-box framework with a subtle universal trigger and claimed theoretical guarantees and stealth properties.
The authors report experimental effectiveness, low clean-accuracy loss, high attack success, and transferability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract reports that exploiting ambiguous or sparse decision-boundary regions can enable substantial misclassification with very few relabeled or poisoned samples.

interpretation.claim: Attack leverage may depend more on the geometry and ambiguity of vulnerable boundaries than on the total number of poisoned samples.

application.claim: For robustness analysis, examine decision-boundary margins and parameter sensitivity in addition to measuring poison rates and clean accuracy.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the reported boundary mechanism generalizes beyond the evaluated models, datasets, and scenarios.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the model architectures, datasets, scenarios, or experimental protocols.
The abstract does not provide details of the theoretical assumptions or proofs behind the stated guarantees.
The abstract does not identify the baselines or define how attack success, stealth, and transferability were measured.
